## Setting
Selection of a redevelopment plan for a central municipal park. A five-person review panel appointed by a city government examines the redevelopment plans prepared for a central park. - Upkeep ledger spend per hectare
- Regional firms tendering for earth-moving
- Depot phasing notes on hoarding the site
- Record of the eastern avenue planting
- Condition of works from the earlier programme
- Timed counts of weekday crossings
- Drainage callouts and August heat readings
- Groundskeeping roll and bought-in services
- Volunteer groups working with the division

The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Kenji, Benjamin, Minato, Minako and Jonathan. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). Name: Kenji
Age: 12
Gender: male
Personality: Kenji is curious and actively takes on challenges. He values his friends and enjoys communicating with those around him. Although he can be a little clumsy at times, he is always positive and never abandons those in need. He is easygoing and well-liked by those around him.

Each participant's part:
- Kenji: Concerned with construction timelines and soil stability. He focuses on the feasibility of the physical works.

Selection of a redevelopment plan for a central municipal park. A five-person review panel appointed by a city government examines the redevelopment plans prepared for a central park. - **Minato**: I agree with Benjamin. I wonder who will take care of the park after it is finished? I want to know if there are enough people to keep it beautiful every day.
- **Minako**: I agree with the need for realism. However, we should look at the actual longevity of previous projects. Blueprints often hide future decay, so I want to see how past works are holding up today.
- **Jonathan**: I agree with all of you. To ensure the park remains a sanctuary without draining the city's coffers, I believe we must look closely at the actual long-term costs of upkeep and maintenance.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Kenji**: That makes sense! To figure out the construction side, I'll look into the regional firms tendering for earth-moving and the depot phasing notes on hoarding the site. That should show us if the timeline is realistic.
- **Benjamin**: I shall complement your focus on logistics with a look at the ground truth. I'll examine the timed counts of weekday crossings and the drainage callouts and August heat readings to see how the site actually behaves.
- **Minato**: I want to see who is helping now. I will look into the groundskeeping roll and bought-in services, and also the volunteer groups working with the division. I hope we find many kind people.
- **Minako**: To assess the actual quality of the city's commissions, I will look into the condition of works from the earlier programme and the record of the eastern avenue planting. I want to see the results.

#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Kenji**: I think we've covered all the bases! We have the construction, the usage, the staffing, the quality, and the money. I'm really curious to see what the earth-moving firms say about the site.
- **Benjamin**: Indeed, we have cast a wide net. I suspect the data on drainage and foot traffic will provide a sobering contrast to the optimism of the architectural renderings. I look forward to the revelations.
- **Minato**: I hope the people who work there are happy. It would be nice if the new plan makes it easier for everyone to help each other and keep the park a peaceful place.
- **Minako**: It is important that we remain objective. Once we have the data, we can determine which plan is truly sustainable rather than just visually appealing. I look forward to seeing the actual state of previous works.
- **Jonathan**: I agree. Let us hope the data provides a clear path forward. I believe a realistic understanding of the financial burden will help us choose a plan that is truly sustainable for the city.

- **Kenji**: I'm ready! Let's see what we find out. I'll be cheering for a plan that actually gets finished on time! See you all in the next round!

- **Minako**: I am ready as well. Let us proceed to the findings. I will be looking for the truth in the results, not the promises in the plans. See you in the next round.

### Findings
- Condition of works from the earlier programme: The overflow basin cut upstream eight years back still needs no rebuild, while the apron resurfaced outside the civic hall in the same programme has been patched three times.

### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4

- **Benjamin**: It seems the earth is as stubborn as the bureaucracy. My findings are equally sobering: the site is a heat trap, and the drainage is failing. Moreover, people are carving their own paths to the tram.
- **Minato**: I found out that there are only seven people on the groundskeeping roll now, which is much fewer than before. But I was happy to see that some kind volunteers are already helping out on weekends!
- **Minako**: My findings confirm a pattern of poor longevity. While some structural work holds, the surface finishes are failing, and half the eastern avenue trees died due to negligent aftercare contracts. We cannot trust the drawings alone.

- **Minato**: @Jonathan, it sounds like the plants are very expensive to look after. Since there are so few groundskeepers left, I worry that the plants might get sad and die like the trees Minako mentioned.

- **Kenji**: I agree! We should look for a plan that uses those durable materials Minako mentioned. If we keep the earth-moving simple, we can avoid those slippage risks and actually finish the project on time!
- **Benjamin**: Logic dictates that we prioritize a design that accommodates the tram commuters' shortcuts rather than fighting them. A plan that ignores these "desire lines" will simply result in trampled greenery and wasted funds.
- **Minato**: I think we should also look for a plan that the volunteers can help with. Since there are so few staff, maybe the kind people who already help can take care of the park together.
- **Minako**: That is a helpful suggestion, Minato. However, we must be careful not to rely solely on volunteers for critical care. We need a design that is fundamentally robust and easy to maintain.
- **Jonathan**: I agree with Minako. While volunteers are a blessing, the city's budget must be the foundation. We should be wary of any plan that maximizes planting just to capture the habitat fund if it creates an unsustainable long-term deficit.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Kenji**: I'm on board! Let's find a plan that's simple to build, doesn't fight the soil, and is easy to keep up. I can't wait to see the candidates and pick the best one!
- **Benjamin**: Indeed. Let us hope the candidates offer a pragmatic approach. A design that respects the heat, the water, and the pedestrians will be the only one that truly survives the first year. I am ready.
- **Minato**: I hope the plans have a way to make the workers and volunteers feel happy and not too tired. I'm looking forward to seeing which one is the most gentle and sustainable for everyone.
- **Minako**: I am also ready. We have a clear set of criteria now: structural durability, realistic maintenance, and a design that respects the site's physical constraints. I will vote for the plan that proves most resilient.
- **Jonathan**: I am also ready. I will be looking for a balance that secures necessary funding without compromising the city's future financial stability. Let us evaluate the candidates with a clear eye for sustainability.
## Round 3
### Options
- A: Wetland Restoration. A plan that reshapes the park's drainage into a series of ponds and reed beds, with boardwalks and observation points arranged along the water's edge.
- B: Market Plaza. A plan that creates a paved central square with stall infrastructure, shade structures, and utility connections intended for weekend markets and seasonal events.
- C: Woodland Walk. A plan that plants dense tree cover across the northern half of the site, threaded with gravel paths, small clearings, and a visitor shelter near the main gate.
- D: Sports Terraces. A plan that replaces the open lawn with multi-use courts, a marked running loop, changing facilities, and stepped seating along the southern side of the site.
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Kenji**: Looking at these, Plan B seems safest! A paved plaza means less deep digging and no worrying about clay slippage. It's way more realistic to finish on time than digging ponds or planting a whole forest!
- **Benjamin**: While Plan B is structurally safe, it may exacerbate the heat trap I discovered. However, Plan A's ponds could be a disaster given the current drainage failures and clay slippage. We need a balance of utility and resilience.
- **Minato**: I think Plan B or D might be better because they have more hard surfaces. Since there are only seven groundskeepers, they won't have to work so hard to keep it beautiful.
- **Minako**:

response: Plan A and C are too risky. Given the history of dead trees and failing surfaces, dense planting and complex water features will likely become ruins. Plan B or D are more realistic for our capacity.

Selection of a redevelopment plan for a central municipal park. A five-person review panel appointed by a city government examines the redevelopment plans prepared for a central park. - Volunteer groups working with the division

The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Kenji, Benjamin, Minato, Minako and Jonathan. | Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |

| 3 | everyone is told the candidates | 4 turns | every participant votes; the candidate with the most votes is selected |

After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

Name: Minato

- Minato: Concerned with the human resources available for upkeep. He looks for options that align with current staffing and volunteers.
